catalog_quote: [p.57] Swahili 語など少数の言語を除き, ほとんどの Bantu 諸語は声調言語で, その多くが音韻的声調を持つ(Kisseberth and Odden 2003: 59). ベンデ語も大多数の Bantu 諸語と同様, 意味の区別に弁別的な声調を持つ. ... [p.59] 語幹ないし語根の声調型には 3 種類あり, それぞれ H(igh) 型, L(ow) 型, 0 型と呼ぶことにする. H 型は語幹ないし語根が H で始まるもの, L 型は語幹ないし語根が L で始まるもの, 0 型は後ろから 2 番目の音節が H となり最終音節は再び L となるものである. 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される. ... 声調規則 1 語幹, 語根の基本的な実現声調 [1σ 2σ 3σ 4σ以上 例(2σ語根)]: H 型 H HH HHH HHHH -bhá.mbá (皮を)張る; L 型 R LH LHH LHHH -bha.ndá 突っつく; 0 型 R RL/HL LHL LLHL -soó.ka 降りる.

new_statements.quote: Guthrie (1948) によるバントゥ諸語の参照番号は F12 であり、相互理解が可能な近接の言語に F11 のトングェ語がある。多くの話者が、両言語は兄弟関係にあり非常に近いという。…ベンデ語の声調は、決して例は多くないが、語彙的および文法的弁別機能を持つ。音節ごとに高声調 H(igh)、低声調 L(ow)、上昇声調 R(ising)、下降声調 F(alling) の 4 種類の実現声調がある…ベンデ語の声調は、音節数が増えてもパターンが限定的であり、基本的には 3 パターンである。すなわち、(a) 語幹がすべて H、(b) 接頭辞は H で語幹が L あるいは R ではじまるもの、(c) は接頭辞が L で語幹の次末音節に H ないし H を含む R や F が現れるものである。
new_statements.translation: Its Guthrie (1948) reference number is F12, and a neighbouring, mutually intelligible language is Tongwe, F11. Many speakers say the two languages are siblings and very close. ... Bende tone, though examples are by no means numerous, has lexical and grammatical distinctive function. Each syllable carries one of four surface tones: High, Low, Rising, Falling ... Bende tone patterns remain limited even as syllable count increases; basically there are three: (a) stem all H; (b) prefix H with the stem beginning in L or R; (c) prefix L with H (or an R/F containing H) appearing on the penultimate syllable of the stem.
new_statements.citation: 阿部優子 [Abe, Yuko]. 2021. ベンデ語の声調 [Tone in Bende]. In 梶茂樹 (ed.), アフリカ諸語の声調・アクセント [Tone and Accent in African Languages], ch.12, pp. 249-278. Tokyo: ILCAA, Tokyo University of Foreign Studies.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: extracted text of p.249 (pdf p.1, sec.1 'ベンデ語の背景') contains every clause of the quoted Japanese verbatim; the '…' marks cover two omitted stretches (speaker-count sentence + scope sentence; 'があるが、本稿では…その結果、'). The (a)/(b)/(c) three-pattern summary recurs verbatim on p.272 (sec.5 intro) as the locator says. Translation is faithful. I also a full-text search for stress/accent the whole chapter for アクセント/強勢/ストレス/stress/accent: the only hit is the project title in fn.1 ('声調・アクセントの総合的研究'); the chapter never characterises Bende (let alone Tongwe) in stress/accent terms, so 'tone language, no stress statement' is the right reading OF THIS SOURCE. Nakamura et al. 2017 p.222 (tong1320/)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand prosodic description is of the Bende variety (bend1258), which Abe treats as one language with Tongwe: a restricted tone system with lexically assigned tonal types (H, L, 0), where one class surfaces with H on the stem penult; nothing is said about word stress, and no phonological study of Tongwe proper exists (Nakamura et al. 2017: 222, saved in tong1320/).
new_statements.exceptions: Abe notes R and F surface tones are positionally restricted (sec. 3.3) and that phrase/sentence tone is uninvestigated; loan-type (0) words pattern with penult H per the 2006 thesis abstract summary. None of this is stated for Tongwe itself.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms of nouns and verbal gerunds (引用形); phrase-level tone explicitly not studied. Statement applies to Bende (F12) data from Katavi Region, not to Tongwe (F11) speech.
new_statements.identity_note: No phonological description of Tongwe proper (tong1320, F11) exists; Nakamura et al. 2017: 222 say so explicitly. The quoted statement describes Bende (bend1258, F12), which Abe (2006 thesis; 2021) defines as one language with Tongwe ('two varieties of one language', mutually intelligible). Glottolog and ISO keep them apart (tny vs bdp). Any catalog entry built from Abe would be a Bende entry, not a Tongwe one.

new_statements.quote: [p.269] 序章に述べたように, 本論ではベンデとトングウェを 1 つの言語の 2 方言として扱った. 両者の違いは, 若干の語彙的なものと, 未来否定の動詞活用形(5 章 2.2.3. 参照)に限られている. その他の点については, 声調を含めて同じである. [p.7] 基礎語彙の語彙統計の比較では, 200 の基礎語のうち, 93%が一致, それも同系の一致というだけでなく, 声調, 音価ともに完全に一致している. [p.57] ベンデ語も大多数の Bantu 諸語と同様, 意味の区別に弁別的な声調を持つ. [p.59] 語幹ないし語根の声調型には 3 種類あり, それぞれ H(igh) 型, L(ow) 型, 0 型と呼ぶことにする. H 型は語幹ないし語根が H で始まるもの, L 型は語幹ないし語根が L で始まるもの, 0 型は後ろから 2 番目の音節が H となり最終音節は再び L となるものである. 借用語の多くが 0 型で実現される. [p.20, F.11 Tongwe per Guthrie 1967-71 vol.2: 47] Tones : Fully distinctive, but opaque
new_statements.translation: [p.269] As stated in the introduction, this thesis treats Bende and Tongwe as two dialects of one language. The differences between them are limited to a few lexical items and the future-negative verb conjugation (see ch. 5, 2.2.3). In all other respects, including tone, they are the same. [p.7] In the lexicostatistical comparison of basic vocabulary, 93% of the 200 basic words agree, and not merely as cognates: they agree completely in both tone and segmental value. [p.57] Bende, like the great majority of Bantu languages, has tone that is distinctive for meaning. [p.59] Stems and roots have three tonal types, which I call H(igh) type, L(ow) type and 0 type. In the H type the stem/root begins with H, in the L type it begins with L, and in the 0 type the penultimate syllable becomes H and the final syllable is L again. Most loanwords are realised as 0 type. [p.20] (Guthrie's characterisation of F.11 Tongwe, quoted by Abe) Tones: fully distinctive, but opaque.

new_statements.relation_note: Tongwe has no catalog record (in_catalog false). The one existing statement (Abe 2021, Bende tone chapter, reading 'none found') describes Bende as a tone language with three lexical tonal types and no word-stress statement; the 2006 thesis is the same author's primary description and agrees with it (tone language, H/L/0 types, 0 type = penult H, no stress statement) and adds what the 2021 chapter does not: an explicit claim that Tongwe is a dialect of the same language identical 'including tone' (p.269; p.7 with the Tongwe informant named in fn.3), Guthrie's Tongwe-specific 'Tones: fully distinctive, but opaque' (p.20), and that Bende long vowels are not penultimate lengthening (p.30). Not…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The language (Bende-Tongwe, described from Bende data) is a tone language: each nominal stem or verbal root carries one of three lexical tonal types (H, L, 0) and the surface H/L/F/R melody is computed from the type plus the syllable count of the word; the 0 type (mostly loanwords) puts H on the penult and L on the final. Nothing is said about word stress, accent or prominence in the phonology chapter (pp.27-39), the tone chapter's overview (pp.57-59), the tone-rule summary (pp.89-90), the introduction or the conclusion; no term アクセント/強勢 occurs in any page read. Vowel length is lexical or from vowel concatenation (Hyman 2003 types a-b), explicitly not the Swahili-type penultimate lengthening (p.30), so there is no penultimate-prominence effect to read as stress. For Tongwe specifically the thesis claims identity with Bende 'including tone' (p.269) on the basis of a 200-word list checked with one Uvinza speaker (p.7 fn.3), and relays Guthrie's 'Tones: fully distinctive, but opaque' for F.11 (p.20).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress described at all).
new_statements.exceptions: Tonal, not stress, exceptions only: some verb conjugations neutralise the root tonal types and impose a fixed pattern; Anti-Meeussen's Rule deletes the left H of two adjacent Hs; the 0 type (penult H, final L) is the pattern of most loanwords, e.g. kuamua 'to decide' from Swahili counted as four syllables to get penult H (pp.27, 58-59). Dialect differences between Bende and Tongwe are limited to a few lexical items and the future-negative conjugation (pp.269-270).
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Bende (Guthrie F12) from fieldwork in Katuma village, Mpanda District (2000-2005, informants Mashaka, Kaboko, R. and R. Nyundo), and argues (序章 1.5, pp.7-10; 終章 2, pp.269-270) that Bende and Tongwe (F11) are two dialects of one language, differing only in a few lexical items and the future-negative conjugation, 'the same including tone'. Its direct Tongwe evidence is a 200-word basic-vocabulary check done in August 2002 with one speaker from Uvinza, Adija Saidi (b. 1964) (p.7 fn.3), plus informant Kaboko (born Kalya, Tongwe-land, clan múlongá) who checked Bende-Tongwe differences (p.10). The thesis also records Ethnologue 15's note that Tongwe and Bende 'may be dialects of one language' (pp.22-23) and that Tongwe splits into a lakeshore group and an Uvinza-area group (p.10). The only Tongwe-specific prosodic statement is Guthrie's, quoted on p.20.

sources.note: Describes BENDE (F12), stating Tongwe (F11) is a mutually intelligible neighbouring language. Bende tone has lexical and grammatical distinctive function; surface H, L, R, F per syllable; citation-form words fall into three patterns: (a) all-H stem, (b) H prefix + stem beginning L/R, (c) L prefix with H (or R/F containing H) on the stem penult. No statement about word stress/accent; phrase-level tone not investigated.
